In addition to submitting its proposal on the commission structure for transactions conducted through the App Store's in-app purchase (IAP) system within the United States, Apple also filed a motion expressing its willingness to explore a settlement with Epic Games. Details are as follows.

Apple may be ready to settle

Earlier today, Apple submitted its proposal outlining the commission it hopes to collect on transactions completed through payment systems outside the App Store.

The timing of this filing is rather noteworthy, as the Supreme Court simultaneously denied Apple's application, refusing to stay the lower court proceedings while Apple appeals Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers' contempt of court ruling against the company. The underlying issue stems from Apple continuing to charge a 27% commission after being ordered by the court to allow developers to redirect users to external payment methods.

According to Apple's proposed structure, it could collect up to a 15% commission on transactions completed through alternative payment systems. Epic Games objected on the spot, stating that it "believes these fees fall entirely outside the scope of guidance provided by the Ninth Circuit regarding permissible fees."

Although that document garnered most of the attention, Apple also filed another motion today, requesting that Judge Gonzalez Rogers order both parties to attend a settlement conference.

Below is the content of the document (edited for clarity):

This means that Apple's legal team had already contacted Epic's attorneys before filing the motion to discuss the possibility of requesting a settlement conference, but Epic did not agree to Apple's request.

In the document, Apple argues that the court has the authority to order both parties to attend a settlement conference without Epic's consent, adding that the Ninth Circuit itself has also encouraged the parties to reach an agreement on appropriate external link commissions.

The company also stated that "discussing potential settlement options in a confidential, non-adversarial environment would increase the likelihood of reaching a pragmatic solution, thereby avoiding a lengthy remand proceeding."

It is worth noting that this document does not contain Apple's settlement proposals or offers, nor does it constitute a substantive settlement proposal. Apple is actually requesting that the court order both parties to conduct settlement negotiations under the supervision of Magistrate Judge Joseph C. Spero.
